payload.value: The question is functionally narrowing in one direction: major infrastructure providers (AWS, Coinbase, Stripe) are shipping products that treat agents as first-class economic transactors, creating market facts faster than legal frameworks can respond. The "principal-agent" framing is dominant in academic and legal circles, but the operational reality is agents acting as semi-independent economic actors with ex-post liability attribution, not pre-authorized principals.

payload.value: The question has advanced from fringe concern to research-grade problem. The Agentic Risk Standard paper (Google DeepMind, Microsoft Research, Columbia, T54 Labs — April 8/13, 2026) is the first formal academic proposal for a guarantee layer in agentic commerce, drawing on escrow, underwriting, and collateralization from construction/insurance/capital markets. Electronic Payments International (May 7) independently confirmed that even the most comprehensive industry analyses of agentic commerce infrastructure (McKinsey, Visa, Mastercard, AP2) do not address dispute management. The question is open because: (1) no card network has a reason code for 'AI misunderstood my preference'; (2) payment infrastructure is advancing faster than dispute infrastructure; (3) who bears the guarantee cost (model provider, agent platform, payment network, or a new insurer class) is completely unresolved.

payload.value: Payments infrastructure for agent commerce is advancing rapidly (x402, MPP, ACP, AgentCore); dispute infrastructure does not exist. The fork is whether a formal guarantee layer (ARS or equivalent) becomes a prerequisite for enterprise agentic commerce adoption — in which case whoever provides it (insurer, payment network, blockchain escrow) captures a significant value layer — or whether the market self-insures by keeping agents in human-supervised roles until liability is clearer, deferring the dispute layer problem indefinitely.
